top_stories.title: AI sector sell-off: correction or temporary dip?
points: AI and tech stocks sold off heavily following the election amid rising political and regulatory uncertainty.
Semiconductor names like Nvidia and Micron now trade at historically depressed valuations after the decline.
Analysts are split on whether this reflects a genuine structural correction (like the dot-com bust) or temporary repricing of high-growth valuations.
Earnings from AI infrastructure players this week (Applied Materials, Cisco, CoreWeave, Nebius, Taiwan Semiconductor) will test whether strong AI demand translates into sustainable revenue growth.

unique_angles.point: George Noble warns Nvidia may be repeating Cisco's 'fatal dot-com playbook'; Michael Burry reportedly sold 25% of his SMH puts (semiconductor ETF put options, a bearish bet), and Goldman Sachs flagged 'frozen' institutional buyers amid the tech de-risking.

CEO confidence remains strong—AMD's Lisa Su says demand is 'off the charts' and Hilton's Chris Nassetta gave an unusually bullish 2027 outlook—suggesting the real issue is rising compliance/permitting costs (a cost-of-capital shock), not demand destruction; operational projects like Hut 8's data centers, SpaceX, and Tesla robotaxi timelines remain unchanged.

items.title: Inflation & Monetary Policy Week
points: October CPI report due Tuesday is expected to show headline inflation at 3.7%, with airfare posting another notable increase.
Multiple Federal Reserve speakers this week (Goolsbee, Barkin, Schmid, Logan, Daly) will offer guidance on interest-rate direction.
A healthy October jobs report has strengthened arguments for potential rate hikes, creating tension with inflation concerns.
Markets are focused on whether inflation data justifies holding rates higher for longer versus recession risks.

items.title: AI & Technology IPO Activity
points: Anthropic begins its IPO road show this week and may file an updated S-1/A with an initial price range and finalized valuation.
Adobe's MAX event starts Tuesday, showcasing its generative AI (AI that creates new content like text or images) capabilities and product roadmap.
Taiwan Semiconductor's monthly revenue data this week is seen as critical for gauging AI chip demand trends.

items.title: Notable Insider & Corporate Activity
points: Berkshire Hathaway ramped up stock buybacks in Q3 even as profits dipped.
Insider trades were noted at Netflix, Intel, and Visa, suggesting mixed corporate confidence.
A report alleges Nvidia's CEO was romantically involved with an alleged Chinese spy.

items.title: Secondary Risk: Industrial Suppliers
points: If the AI-related sell-off persists, it could ripple to industrial suppliers like Caterpillar that support data center infrastructure buildout.

issues.subject: Morning Brief: AI stocks have been blown up, but keep this in mind

headlines: AI stocks sold off heavily following election results, but company fundamentals remain intact—data center projects will continue, just with higher regulatory hurdles and costs.
AMD CEO reports demand is "off the charts" and Hilton CEO expressed confidence in 2027 outlook, signaling core business momentum persists despite market turbulence.
Earnings estimates for 2027-2028 are no longer reliable due to increased compliance costs for data center buildouts, creating an "adjustment period" rather than structural collapse.
AI infrastructure companies like Nvidia and Micron now trade at historically cheap valuations after the sell-off, potentially presenting entry opportunities for long-term investors.
Political uncertainty will raise project timelines and expenses but won't halt the AI boom—the comparison to the dot-com bust is premature.

sections.title: Why Fundamentals Haven't Collapsed Despite Market Turbulence
points: 1. Operating companies face execution delays and higher permitting costs, not work stoppages—Hut 8's data center buildout continues, SpaceX remains operational, and Tesla robotaxi timelines are unchanged.

2. CEO confidence signals business resilience: AMD's Lisa Su cited off-the-charts demand; Hilton's Chris Nassetta (20-year veteran) shared 2027 guidance he typically withholds, forecasting no dramatic impacts in the next 2-3 years.
3. The U.S. political system's design creates stability—regulatory friction increases costs but doesn't eliminate large-scale infrastructure projects like AI data centers.

sections.title: The Real Market Adjustment: Cost Inflation, Not Demand Destruction
points: 1. Data center projects face a higher bar to approval and will cost more to execute, directly impacting AI ecosystem earnings estimates for 2027-2028, which markets are now repricing.
2. Secondary impacts could ripple to industrial suppliers (e.g., Caterpillar) if the selling persists and slows supporting infrastructure buildout.
3. This represents a cost-of-capital shock to the AI boom timeline, not evidence of a dot-com-style bust or fundamental rejection of AI infrastructure investment.

sections.title: Valuation Opportunity in AI Hardware
points: 1. Nvidia, Micron, and similar semiconductor companies now trade at historically depressed valuations following the sell-off, creating a potential entry point for patient investors.
2. The adjustment period is temporary—once markets price in the regulatory cost increases, recovery can accelerate if execution timelines stabilize.
